opus-5.5.text:
I think there's still quite a lot of headroom. When we released K2, we always said it was a starting point rather than an endpoint. The base model has strong capabilities, but many of them haven't been fully drawn out yet, especially in post-training.

One area is agentic ability. K2 was designed with agentic tasks in mind: tool use, multi-step reasoning, working in real environments. But how well a model performs as an agent depends heavily on how much high-quality interaction data and how many diverse environments you can scale up in reinforcement learning. We're still early there. As we build richer environments and better reward signals, I expect meaningful gains on long-horizon tasks, which matter most for real-world use.

Another area is reasoning, letting the model think longer and more effectively at test time. Combining that kind of extended thinking with agentic behavior, so the model can plan, act, observe, and correct itself, should unlock a lot.

There's also the efficiency side. With things like the optimizer work we did, we found we can get more out of each token of training data. Since high-quality data is becoming the real bottleneck, token efficiency translates directly into intelligence. That gives the same architecture more room to grow.

So my view is that the ceiling of K2 as a foundation is quite high. What we've shown so far is maybe a fraction of what it can do. The question is how fast we can scale RL and environments to bring that potential out.

r001.rationale: The response says K2 was released as a starting point and that its base model’s capabilities remain underdeveloped, especially in post-training, attributing its remaining potential to the released model being closer to a base model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think K2 still has a lot of headroom, and the headroom comes from a few different directions.

The first is simply that the base model is undertrained relative to what it could absorb. We used the MuonClip optimizer to get stable training across fifteen-plus trillion tokens without a single loss spike, and that stability means we could keep scaling tokens and compute and the curve would keep going. We haven't hit a wall on pretraining; we hit a budget.

The second direction is post-training, and that's where I actually think most of the near-term gains are. Agentic data synthesis, reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, tool use at scale. K2 is already decent at these things, but the RL side is still early. If you look at how much the gap between the base model and the instruct model has grown over the past year, that's a signal that the post-training recipe is becoming a bigger and bigger share of the final capability. There's a lot of room to push on self-critique, on longer-horizon tasks, on getting the model to actually learn from its own trajectories rather than from curated data.

The third is context and reasoning. We deliberately released K2 as a non-thinking model first, because we wanted a strong, fast base that people could build agents on. But adding a proper thinking mode on top of this architecture is a fairly natural next step, and from our internal experiments the returns from that are significant, especially on math and code.

So if you ask me how much is left, I'd say we've used maybe a third of what the architecture can do. The one trillion parameter MoE with thirty-two billion active is a good shape. It gives us capacity without making inference unreasonably expensive. The question now is less about whether the model can get better and more about how fast we can run the loop: better data, better RL, better infrastructure, and then feeding that back in.

What I'd caution against is thinking of it as a single number that goes up. Different capabilities will saturate at different rates. Knowledge recall is close to its ceiling for this size. Agentic reliability, the ability to do something fifty steps long without derailing, is nowhere near its ceiling, and that's the thing we care most about.

r001.rationale: The response says K2 was released as a “non-thinking model” and describes it as a strong base, but it does not say the previously released version was closer to a base model.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still substantial room for improvement, but I’d distinguish between getting more out of K2’s existing capabilities and improving the underlying model. The first is about how effectively it works through a problem—whether it can check its reasoning, recognize mistakes, and use feedback. The second is about making those capabilities more reliable through training.

I wouldn’t put a precise ceiling on it. The important question is whether additional effort produces consistent gains on difficult tasks. Solving something once is encouraging; solving it reliably is what makes the capability useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think K2 still has substantial room to improve. I’d separate that into two questions: how much more capability we can develop through training, and how reliably we can turn that capability into useful results. Those aren’t quite the same thing. A model can do well on a difficult problem and still struggle to complete a longer task consistently.

So I wouldn’t judge the remaining potential only by benchmark scores. I’d look at whether it can reason through more steps, use tools effectively, and recognize and correct its own mistakes. The real test is whether it can handle increasingly complex work with less intervention. I wouldn’t put a precise ceiling on that yet.
